newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hongkong Bank takes back seat in new bankers' club.
newsitem.headline: Hongkong Bank takes back seat in new bankers' club.

text.p: Hong Kong's leading bankers launched a club on Thursday to celebrate the British colony's reversion to China later this year, but heavyweight Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corp Ltd was not at the high table.
The territory's largest bank, Hongkong Bank, a unit of London-based HSBC Holdings Plc, was left out of the decision-making tier of the club of bankers and financiers.
The bank, founded in 1865, was once a bastion of the colonial order.
The inauguration of the Hong Kong Financial Community Committee for the Celebration of Reunification of Hong Kong with China was held at the local headquarters of the Bank of China.
Industry watchers have said the bankers on the committee's ruling council could herald a new order in the territory's banking and finance industry.
Banking analysts have said the club committee's structure could reveal the hierarchy of banks in the territory after Britain hands Hong Kong back to China on July 1.
But Hongkong Bank said its relatively low profile in the celebratory committee was not a sign it was being marginalised.

The committee's six chairmen include executives of two China-funded banks: Yang Zilin, chief executive at the Hong Kong-Macau regional office of the Bank of China, and Chuang Shih-ping, honorary chairman of Nanyang Commercial Bank Ltd.

"We wish to promote unity among different financial industries, encourage the financial community to jointly celebrate this historic occassion, and express...our confidence in Hong Kong's future," Yang said at the launch.

The committee brings together more than 500 members of the banking, insurance, securities and other finance industries to celebrate Hong Kong's return to China after more than 150 years of British colonial rule.
Hongkong Bank was not entirely absent -- executive director Vincent Cheng, the bank's highest ranking ethnic Chinese, is one of 20 vice-chairmen but not in the decision-making tier.

Hongkong Bank dominated the financial business of the territory throughout Britain's rule. The saying used to be that the real power in the territory resided in such colonial establishments as the Royal Hong Kong Jockey Club, the Jardine Matheson trading house, and Hongkong Bank.
The bank printed Hong Kong's bank notes, along with fellow British institution Standard Chartered Bank.
But Hongkong Bank is also adjusting to a new reality brought on by the approaching handover and the increasing maturity of Hong Kong's economy.
The formation of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority in 1993 removed most of the bank's former responsibilities as the government's quasi-representative in the financial markets.

The Bank of China also began issuing bank notes in 1994, and in 1996 its local chief took his turn as chairman of the Hong Kong Association of Banks, a position that used to shuttle between Hongkong Bank and Standard Chartered Bank.

Analysts said Hongkong Bank was too big and too good at its job to be marginalised after the handover, nor would it be in China's interests to do so. Hongkong Bank itself has always maintained its post-handover prospects remained good.

"We will continue to invest in Hong Kong and China," HSBC group chairman William Purves said in March during a visit to the territory. "We are taking a positive view rather than a negative view that you see so often in the press."
